en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 14.
Samathakkhandhaka (The Chapter on the Methods for Settling Disputes)
1. Resolution in the Presence.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were performing formal acts against monks who were not present.
[They perform] acts of censure, demotion, banishment, reconciliation, and suspension.
Those monks who are of few desires... they grumble, complain, and protest:
"How can the group-of-six monks perform formal acts against monks who are not present?"
“...the act of censure, the act of demotion, the act of banishment, the act of reconciliation, and the act of suspension.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… [The Buddha said: “Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks perform formal acts against monks who are not present?”
“Is there also the act of censure, the act of demotion, the act of banishment, the act of reconciliation, and the act of suspension?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“Bhikkhus, it is unbecoming, unsuitable, unworthy, improper, unmonkish,
and unfit to be done for those foolish men. How indeed, bhikkhus, can those foolish men carry out formal acts against monks who are not present—
whether acts of censure, demotion, banishment, reconciliation, or suspension?
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“Monks, a formal act— whether one of censure, demotion, banishment, reconciliation, or suspension— must not be carried out against monks who are not present.
Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
An individual who speaks contrary to the Dhamma; several individuals who speak contrary to the Dhamma; a Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma.
An individual who speaks according to the Dhamma; several individuals who speak according to the Dhamma;
a Saṅgha that speaks according to the Dhamma. 1.1. The Ninefold Group on the Dark Side.
A person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, induces, leads, shows, and instructs a person who speaks according to the Dhamma, saying:
“This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya; this is the Teacher’s instruction. Accept this; approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of *saṃmukhā-vinaya*.
A person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, induces, leads, shows, and instructs a number of people who speak according to the Dhamma, saying:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of a *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
A person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, induces, incites, shows, and demonstrates to the Saṅgha that speaks according to the Dhamma, saying:
“This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya; this is the Teacher’s instruction; take up this; approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of *saṃmukhā-vinaya*.
When a number of speakers of what is contrary to the Dhamma persuade, convince, prevail upon, entreat, show, and demonstrate a person who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, saying:
“This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya; this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up;
approve of this,” and if that legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of resolution face-to-face.
When many who speak contrary to the Dhamma cause many who speak in accordance with the Dhamma to recognize, to reflect upon, to consider, to examine, to see, and to understand— saying,
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this”—
if that legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of resolution in the presence of the Sangha.
A number of speakers of what is contrary to the Dhamma persuade, convince, entice, allure, show, and demonstrate a speaker of the Dhamma in the Saṅgha, saying:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in such a way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of a *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
A Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, makes one see, makes one reflect, shows, and demonstrates a person who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, saying:
"This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of resolution face-to-face.
A Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, makes look at, makes look around, shows, and demonstrates many who speak in accordance with the Dhamma, saying:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in such a way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of a resolution face-to-face.
A Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, makes look at, causes to look closely at, shows, and demonstrates a Saṅgha that speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, saying:
“This is the Dhamma; this is the Vinaya; this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up; approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in such a way, it is settled contrary to the Dhamma by means of a semblance of a *saṃmukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
The section on the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) is finished.
1.2. The Section on the Bright Side (sukkapakkha):
A person who speaks according to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, inspires, encourages, shows, and instructs a person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled according to the Dhamma by means of resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*).
A person who speaks according to the Dhamma persuades, convinces, inspires, encourages, shows, and instructs many persons who speak contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled by means of the Dhamma through the *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
A person who speaks according to the Dhamma convinces, persuades, makes look, causes to look closely, shows, and demonstrates a Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled by means of the Dhamma through the *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
A plurality of those who speak according to the Dhamma persuade, convince, examine, re-examine, show, and demonstrate the person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If a legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled according to the Dhamma by means of resolution in the presence of the parties (*saṃmukhāvinaya*).
Many who speak according to the Dhamma persuade, convince, examine, re-examine, show, and demonstrate many who speak contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled by the Dhamma through the *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
When many who speak according to the Dhamma persuade, convince, look on with favor, keep looking on with favor, show, and demonstrate the Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma—
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled by the Dhamma through the *saṃmukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence).
The Saṅgha that speaks according to the Dhamma makes the person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma understand, makes him reflect, makes him consider, makes him examine, shows him, and instructs him.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If a legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled according to the Dhamma by means of resolution in the presence of the parties.
A Saṅgha that speaks according to the Dhamma convinces, persuades, makes see, makes look closely, shows, and demonstrates many who speak contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this.
If the legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled according to the Dhamma by means of resolution face-to-face (*saṃmukhāvinaya*).
The Saṅgha that speaks according to the Dhamma informs, convinces, makes look, makes look closely, shows, and demonstrates to the Saṅgha that speaks contrary to the Dhamma.
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take up this, approve of this.
If this legal issue is settled in this way, it is settled by means of the Dhamma through the presence of the parties (sammukhāvinaya).
Thus ends the ninefold section on the bright side.
2. The Settlement by Confession (Sativinaya).
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta had realized Arhatship at the age of seven.
Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by him;
there is nothing further for him to do, nor anything to be added to what has been done.
Then, while the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Indeed, when I was seven years old, I realized arhatship.
Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by me.
There is nothing further for me to do, nor is there any need to add to what has been done.”
“What service might I perform for the Saṅgha?
Then it occurred to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“What if I were to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and assign meals?”
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta said this to the Blessed One:
"Just now, Bhante, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:..."
“Indeed, by me at the age of seven, arahantship was realized.
Whatever can be attained by a disciple has all been attained by me.
There is nothing further for me to do, nor is there any need for the re-doing of what has been done.”
"What service indeed might I perform for the Saṅgha?
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
"What if I were to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate meals for them?"
“Venerable sir, I wish to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and to designate meals.
“Excellent, excellent, Dabba!
Therefore, Dabba, you should arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and designate meals.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha appoint Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.”
And furthermore, monks, he should be appointed in this way.
First, Dabba Mallaputta should be requested.
Having requested him, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the venerable Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
This is the motion.’
"Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs.
The Sangha appoints the venerable Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
Whosoever among the venerable ones approves of the appointment of the venerable Dabba Mallaputta as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals, let him be silent."
"Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The venerable Dabba Mallaputta has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the assigner of lodgings and the distributor of meals.
It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this."
And the venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having been appointed, assigned lodgings together for the bhikkhus who were like-minded.
He assigned lodgings together for those bhikkhus who were experts in the Suttas, thinking:
"They will recite the Suttas together."
He assigns lodgings together for those bhikkhus who are experts in the Vinaya, thinking:
"They will resolve matters of the Vinaya among themselves.
He assigns lodgings together for those bhikkhus who are preachers of the Dhamma.
“They will discuss the Dhamma with one another.
He assigns lodgings together for those monks who are meditators, thinking:
“They will not disturb one another.”
To those monks who were given to frivolous talk and who lived with much physical rigidity, he assigned lodgings all together,
thinking, "In this way, these venerable ones will pass the night.
And to those monks who arrived at an improper time, he would enter the fire-element and assign them lodgings by that very light.
Furthermore, monks would intentionally arrive at the wrong time,
thinking, "We shall see the miracle of psychic power performed by the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta.
Having approached the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, they spoke to him thus:
“Friend Dabba, please assign us lodgings.
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta replied to them, “Venerable sirs, where do you wish [to stay]? Where shall I assign them?”
They intentionally made excuses from afar, saying:
"Friend Dabba, assign lodgings for us on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Friend, assign lodgings for us at the Robbers' Precipice."
"Friend, prepare a lodging for us on the Black Rock on the slope of Isigili.
Friend, prepare a lodging for us in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the slope of Vebhāra.
Friend, prepare a lodging for us in the Sappasoṇḍika Cave in the Cool Grove."
"Friend, please prepare lodgings for us at Gotamaka Cave.
Friend, please prepare lodgings for us at Tinduka Cave.
Friend, please prepare lodgings for us at Tapoda Cave."
“Friend, please prepare lodgings for us in the Tapodārāma.
Friend, please prepare lodgings for us in Jīvakambavana.
Friend, please prepare lodgings for us in the Migadāya at Maddakucchi.”
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having entered the fire-element attainment, went ahead of them with his finger blazing.
They also followed behind the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta by that very light.
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta assigned lodgings to them in this way:

“This is the bed, this is the chair, this is the mattress, this is the pillow, this is the place for excrement, this is the place for urine, this is the drinking water, this is the water for washing, this is the walking stick; this is the Sangha’s agreement on the rules:
one must enter at this time, and one must leave at this time.”
When the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta had thus assigned lodgings for them, he returned once again to the Bamboo Grove.
Now at that time, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka were both junior and of little merit;
consequently, they received whatever lodgings were inferior among those belonging to the Saṅgha, as well as inferior meals.
Now at that time, people in Rājagaha desired to give specially prepared almsfood to the elder bhikkhus—
ghee, oil, and additional curry—
but they gave ordinary food to the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
They ate whatever was available, such as broken rice with sour gruel and fermented rice-scum.
After returning from their alms round following the meal, they asked the elder bhikkhus, "Friends, what did you get in the dining hall? What did you get?"
Some elders spoke thus:
"Friends, we had ghee, we had oil, we had supplementary food.
But the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka bhikkhus spoke thus:
“Friends, we had nothing at all—
just ordinary food as it was cooked, consisting of broken rice with sour gruel as the second course.
Now at that time, a householder who provided fine meals was giving a regular meal of four dishes to the Saṅgha.
Thus, at the meal hall, he attended to them together with his wife and children and served them:
some asked for rice, some asked for soup, some asked for oil, and some asked for additional side dishes.
Now at that time, a meal for the following day had been assigned by the householder Kalyāṇabhattika to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
Then the householder Kalyāṇabhattika went to the monastery on some business.
He approached the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, and having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta and sat down to one side.
As the householder Kalyāṇabhattika was sitting there, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then the householder Kalyāṇabhattika, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
"Venerable sir, for whom has the meal for tomorrow been designated at our house?
"Householder, the meal for tomorrow at your house has been designated for the monks from Mettiya and Bhūmajaka."
Then the householder Kalyāṇabhattika became displeased.
Thinking, "How can these wicked bhikkhus eat in our house? he went home and commanded his slave girl:
"Girl, when those who are invited for tomorrow's meal arrive, arrange seats at the gateway and serve them with broken rice and sour gruel."
“Yes, noble sirs,” that slave girl replied to the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.
Then the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka thought,
“Yesterday, friends, we were assigned the meal at the householder Kalyāṇabhattika’s.”
"Our own benefactor, the householder Kalyāṇabhattika, will attend upon us along with his wife and children and serve us;
some will ask for rice, some for soup, some for oil, and others for additional side dishes.
With that very joy, they did not sleep soundly during the night.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka dressed, took their bowls and robes, and went to the residence of the householder Kalyāṇabhattika.
The female slave saw the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka coming from afar;
seeing them, she prepared a seat at the gateway and said this to the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka:
“Sit down, venerable sirs.
Then it occurred to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka:
“Without a doubt, the meal has not yet been prepared, since we have been made to sit at the gateway.”
Then that female slave approached them with broken rice and sour gruel, saying,
"Eat, venerable sirs.
"We are those who receive regular meals, sister," they replied.
“I know, noble ladies, that you are those who eat regularly.
However, yesterday I was instructed by the householder:
‘Friends, whatever regular diners come tomorrow, prepare seats for them at the gateway and serve them broken rice with sour gruel as the second course.’”
“Eat, venerable sir.
Then the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka thought,
“Friends, yesterday the householder Kalyāṇabhattika went to the monastery to see Dabba Mallaputta.”
“Without a doubt, we have been alienated from the householder Dabba Mallaputta.
Because of that very dejection, they did not eat their meals with a proper mind.
Then, after the meal, when they had returned from the almsround, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka went to the monastery.

Having put away their bowls and robes, they sat down outside the monastery gate, folding their upper robes as a seat, silent, abashed, with shoulders drooping and heads cast down, brooding and speechless.
Then the bhikkhunī Mettiyā approached the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka; having approached them, she said this to the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka:
“I pay homage, venerable ladies.
When this was said, the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka did not speak to him.
A second time... [as before]...
A third time, the bhikkhunī Mettiyā said this to the bhikkhus of Mettiyabhūma:
“I pay homage, venerable sirs.
A third time, the bhikkhus of Mettiyabhūma did not speak to her.
“Have I offended the noble ladies?
Why do the noble ladies not speak to me?
“Because, sister, you remained indifferent while we were being harassed by Dabba Mallaputta.”
“What can I do, noble ladies?
“If you so wished, sister, the Blessed One would have expelled Venerable Dabba Mallaputta this very day.
“What can I do, noble ladies?”
"What can I do? [He replied:
"Come, sister, approach the Blessed One, and having approached, speak thus to the Blessed One:
'Venerable sir, this is not covered over and is not fitting: that which was a direction free from fear, calamity, and distress has now become a direction full of fear, calamity, and distress.'"
“Where there was no wind, there is now a wind;
I think the water is on fire!
I have been ruined by the noble Dabba Mallaputta.”
“Yes, noble lady,” the bhikkhunī Mettiyā replied to the bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka. She then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side.
Standing there, the bhikkhunī Mettiyā said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this is neither well-covered nor appropriate: that which was a direction free from fear, calamity, and distress has now become a direction full of fear, calamity, and distress.”
"Where there was no wind, there is now a wind;
I think the water is on fire!
I have been defiled by the noble Dabba Mallaputta."
Then, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Do you recall, Dabba, doing such a thing as this nun has described?
“I do not recall, Bhante, doing anything of which the Blessed One would know me.”
A second time, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Dabba, do you remember doing such a thing as this nun has described?
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One know me according to my actual nature.”
A third time, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta:
“Dabba, do you recall doing such a thing as this nun has described?
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows me as I am.”
“Dabba, the Dabbas do not evade in this way.
If it was done by you, say ‘It was done.
If it was not done, say ‘It was not done.’”
“Venerable sir, since I was born, I do not recall having engaged in sexual intercourse even in a dream, much less while awake.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, expel the bhikkhunī Mettiyā.”
"And you, monks, should apply yourselves to these.
Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then those monks expelled the nun Mettiyā.
Then the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka said this to those monks:
"Friends, do not expel the nun Mettiyā; she has committed no offense.
She was incited by us when we were angry, displeased, and intent on her removal."
“But why, friends, have you groundlessly accused the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta of a failure in virtue?
“It is so, friend.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How can the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka actually baselessly charge the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a failure in virtue?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka have baselessly charged Dabba Mallaputta with a failure in virtue?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
Having rebuked them … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha grant the settlement by way of mindfulness (sativinaya) to Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness.
And this, monks, is how it should be granted:
Let that Dabba Mallaputta approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, and...
Having done so, having bowed at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, having sat down in the kneeling posture (ukkuṭika), and having raised his joined palms (añjali), he should speak to them thus:
‘Venerable sirs, these bhikkhus Mettiya and Bhūmajaka are groundlessly charging me with a failure in moral discipline.
Therefore, venerable sirs, having attained fullness of mindfulness, I request the Saṅgha for a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya).’”
He should be asked a second time;
he should be asked a third time:
“Venerable sirs, these monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka are groundlessly charging me with a failure in virtue.”
‘Thus, having attained fullness of mindfulness, for a third time, venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha for a verdict of mindfulness.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
These monks from Mettiya and Bhūmajja are groundlessly charging the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a failure in virtue.
The venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having attained fullness of mindfulness, requests the Saṅgha for a verdict of mindfulness.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a verdict of mindfulness to the venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs.
These monks, Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, are groundlessly charging the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a failure in moral conduct.
The Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having attained fullness of mindfulness, requests a verdict of mindfulness from the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha grants a verdict of mindfulness to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness.
Whoever among the Venerable Ones approves of granting a verdict of mindfulness to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
For the second time I state this matter... for the third time I state this matter: [whoever does not approve of this, let him speak].
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
These monks, Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, are groundlessly charging the venerable Dabba Mallaputta with a failure in moral conduct.
The venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having attained fullness of mindfulness, requests the Saṅgha for a verdict of mindfulness."
The Saṅgha grants the resolution through mindfulness to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness.
Whichever Venerable approves of granting the resolution through mindfulness to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“The Saṅgha has granted a verdict of mindfulness to the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, who has attained fullness of mindfulness.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
“Monks, there are these five lawful ways of granting a verdict of mindfulness.”

“A bhikkhu is pure and free from offense, yet they accuse him; he requests [a formal act], and the Saṅgha grants him a verdict of mindfulness (sativinaya) in accordance with the Dhamma by a unanimous assembly.
These, monks, are the five legitimate ways of granting a verdict of mindfulness. 3.
Verdict of Past Insanity (Amūḷhavinaya)
Now at that time, the bhikkhu Gagga was insane, his mind deranged.
While he was insane and deranged, he committed many things unbecoming of a monastic and spoke many such words.
The bhikkhus reproved the bhikkhu Gagga for an offense on account of what had been committed by him while he was insane and deranged.
“Did the Venerable One commit such an offense?
He replies thus:
“Friend, I was indeed insane, my mind was deranged.”
"Because of that madness of mine, which caused a perversion of my mind, I have committed and spoken many things unworthy of a recluse.
I do not remember those things;
they were done by me while I was deluded."
Even when addressed in this way, they still accused him, saying:
"Does the venerable one remember having committed such an offense?
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, complained, and became vexed.
“How indeed can the monks reprove the monk Gagga for an offense committed while he was insane and mentally deranged, saying:
‘Does the venerable one remember having committed such an offense?

What are the three wholesome roots that are the root of a legal issue arising from censure?

What is the root of a legal issue arising from an offense?
The six origins of offenses are the root of a legal issue arising from an offense.
There is an offense that originates from the body, not from speech, nor from the mind.
There is an offense that originates from speech, not from the body, nor from the mind.
There is an offense that originates from both the body and speech, but not from the mind.
There is an offense that originates from both body and mind, but not from speech.

These six origins of offenses are the root of the legal issue arising from an offense.
What is the root of the legal issue arising from business?
There is one root for the legal issue arising from business:
The Saṅgha.
A legal issue arising from a dispute may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
A legal issue arising from a dispute may be wholesome, it may be unwholesome, or it may be indeterminate.
In this regard, what is a legal issue arising from a dispute that is wholesome?
Here, monks, monks with wholesome minds dispute:
"It is Dhamma" or "It is non-Dhamma," and so forth...
Whether it be "an offense of a grave nature" or "an offense not of a grave nature"—

In that regard, what is a legal issue arising from a dispute that is unwholesome?
Here, monks, monks with unwholesome minds dispute:
"It is Dhamma" or "It is not Dhamma," and so forth...
Whether it be "an offense of a grave nature" or "an offense not of a grave nature"—
whatever quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, variance of opinion, speaking otherwise, contentious speech, or wrangling occurs therein—
this is called an unwholesome legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
In this regard, what is a legal issue arising from a dispute that is indeterminate?
Here, monks, monks with indeterminate minds dispute:
"It is Dhamma" or "It is not Dhamma," and so forth...
Whether it be "an offense of a grave nature" or "an offense not of a grave nature"—
whatever quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, variance of opinion, speaking otherwise, contentious talk, or wrangling occurs therein—
this is called an undetermined legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇaṃ abyākatam*).
The legal issue of accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*) is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
The legal issue of accusation may be wholesome, it may be unwholesome, or it may be indeterminate.
In this regard, what is the legal issue of accusation that is wholesome?
"Furthermore, monks, here monks with unwholesome minds reprove another monk for failure in virtue,
or failure in conduct, or failure in view, or failure in livelihood. Whatever therein is reproving,
reproaching, upbraiding, censuring, compliance, encouragement, or lending support— this is called 'reproving'."
This is called a legal issue arising from censure that is wholesome.
In this regard, what is a legal issue arising from censure that is unwholesome?
Here, monks, monks with unwholesome minds censure another monk.
Whether it be through failure in virtue, failure in conduct, failure in view,
or failure in livelihood; whatever therein is reproach, censuring, misrepresentation, speaking against, compliance, encouragement, or providing support—
this is called an unwholesome legal issue arising from reproach (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
In this regard, what is a legal issue of reproach that is indeterminate?
Here, monks, monks reproach a monk with an indeterminate mind—
either for failure in virtue, or for failure in conduct, or for failure in view, or for failure in livelihood.
Whatever there is therein of reproaching, reproaching, speaking in favor of, speaking along with, compliance, encouragement, and lending support—
this is called an indeterminate legal issue arising from reproach (*anuvādādhikaraṇaṃ abyākataṃ*).
Is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇaṃ*) wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
The legal issue arising from an offense may be unwholesome, and it may be indeterminate;
there is no legal issue arising from an offense that is wholesome.
In this regard, what is the legal issue arising from an offense that is unwholesome?
When one transgresses while knowing, perceiving, intending, and having deliberately resolved—
this is called an unwholesome legal issue arising from an offense.
In that regard, what is an indeterminate legal issue arising from an offense?
That transgression which occurs without knowing, without perceiving, without intending, and without having resolved upon it—
this is called an indeterminate legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
Is a legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
A legal issue arising from business may be wholesome, it may be unwholesome, or it may be indeterminate.
In this regard, what is a legal issue arising from business that is wholesome?
It is when the Saṅgha performs an act with a wholesome mind.
A formal act of obtaining permission, a formal act consisting of a motion, a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation, and a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations—
this is called a wholesome legal issue arising from business.
In this regard, what is an unwholesome legal issue arising from business?
When the Saṅgha performs an act with an unwholesome mind— whether it be an act of notification,
an act consisting of one motion, an act consisting of a motion and a second resolution, or an act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution—
this is called an unwholesome legal issue concerning business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
In this context, what is a legal issue arising from business that is indeterminate?
It is when the Saṅgha performs an act with an indeterminate mind—
whether it be an act of notification, an act consisting of a motion, an act consisting of a motion and one proclamation, or an act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
This is called an indeterminate legal issue concerning duty (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
Dispute is a legal issue concerning dispute; there is dispute that is not a legal issue, there is a legal issue that is not dispute, and there is that which is both a legal issue and dispute.

There may be dispute that is a legal issue concerning dispute; there may be dispute that is not a legal issue; there may be a legal issue that is not dispute; and there may be that which is both a legal issue and dispute.
In this regard, what is dispute as a legal issue arising from dispute?
Here, monks, monks dispute:
"It is Dhamma" or "It is non-Dhamma"... [and so on].
Whether it be "this is a grave offense" or "this is not a grave offense"—
whatever quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, disagreement, speaking otherwise, contentious speech, or wrangling occurs therein— this is a dispute,
a legal issue arising from a dispute.
In this regard, what is a dispute that is not a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*)?
A mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother; a father disputes with his son, and a son disputes with his father;
a brother disputes with a brother, and a brother disputes with a sister; a sister [disputes with a brother]...
Brothers dispute, and even companions dispute with their companions—
this is a dispute that is not a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
In this regard, what is a legal issue that is not a dispute?
The legal issue of reproval, the legal issue of an offense, and the legal issue of business—
this is a legal issue that is not a dispute.
In this regard, what is a legal issue that is both a legal issue and a dispute?
A legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is both a legal issue and a dispute.

A formal accusation (*anuvāda*) may be a legal issue arising from an accusation, it may be an accusation that is not a legal issue, it may be a legal issue that is not an accusation, or it may be both a legal issue and an accusation.

It may be an accusation that is a legal issue arising from an accusation; it may be an accusation that is not a legal issue; it may be a legal issue that is not an accusation; or it may be both a legal issue and an accusation.
In this regard, what is a reproach that constitutes a legal issue arising from reproach?
Here, monks, monks reprove another monk—
either for failure in virtue, or for failure in conduct, or for failure in view, or for failure in livelihood.
Whatever there is therein of reproaching, reproaching, misrepresenting, reviling, compliance, encouragement, and providing support— this is reproach,
this is a legal issue arising from reproach (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
In that regard, what is reproach that is not a legal issue?
The mother reproaches the son, and the son reproaches the mother; the father reproaches the son, and the son reproaches the father;
the brother reproaches the brother, the brother reproaches the sister, the sister reproaches the brother, and the companion reproaches the companion.
This is an accusation, not a legal issue.
In this context, what is a legal issue that is not an accusation?
It is a legal issue arising from an offense, a legal issue arising from business, and a legal issue arising from a dispute.
This legal issue is not an accusation.
In this context, what is both a legal issue and an accusation?
A legal issue arising from an accusation is both a legal issue and an accusation.
An offense is a legal issue arising from an offense; an offense is not a legal issue; a legal issue is not an offense; and a legal issue is both a legal issue and an offense.

It may be that an offense is a legal issue arising from an offense; it may be that an offense is not a legal issue; it may be that a legal issue is not an offense; and it may be that a legal issue is both a legal issue and an offense.
In this regard, what is an offense that is a legal issue arising from an offense?
The five classes of offenses are a legal issue arising from an offense; the seven classes of offenses are a legal issue arising from an offense.
This is an offense that is a legal issue.
In this context, what is an offense that is not a legal issue?
The attainment of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-samāpatti*):
this is an offense, not a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
In that regard, what is a legal issue, not an offense?
The legal issue arising from business, the legal issue arising from dispute, and the legal issue arising from censure—
this is a legal issue that is not an offense.
In this regard, what is a legal issue that is also an offense?
A legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is both a legal issue and an offense.

Regarding what is to be done (*kicca*): there is that which is a legal issue arising from what is to be done (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), that which is what is to be done but not a legal issue, that which is a legal issue but not what is to be done, and that which is both a legal issue and what is to be done.

It may be that what is to be done is a legal issue arising from what is to be done; it may be that what is to be done is not a legal issue; it may be that a legal issue is not what is to be done; and it may be that it is both a legal issue and what is to be done.
In this context, what is a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*)?

Whatever constitutes the business or duty of the Saṅgha, whether it be a formal act consisting of a mere motion (*apalokanakamma*), a formal act consisting of a single motion (*ñattikamma*), a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), or a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*)—
this is a legal issue arising from business.
In this context, what is a duty that is not a legal issue?
The duty toward a teacher, the duty toward a preceptor, the duty toward one who has the same preceptor, and the duty toward one who has the same teacher—
this is a duty that is not a legal issue.
In this regard, what is a legal issue that is not a duty?
A dispute as a legal issue, an accusation as a legal issue, and an offense as a legal issue—
this is a legal issue that is not a duty.
In this context, what is that which is both a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) and a duty (*kicca*)?
A legal issue concerning duties (*kiccādhikaraṇa*) is both a legal issue and a duty.
9. The Settling of Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇavūpasamana-samatha*).
9.1. Resolution Face-to-Face:
By how many methods of settlement is a legal issue arising from a dispute settled?
A legal issue arising from a dispute is settled by two methods of settlement: [namely, resolution face-to-face and resolution through majority decision].
By means of resolution face-to-face and by means of majority decision.
Could a legal issue arising from a dispute be settled by one method of settling, without resorting to the method of majority decision—
that is, by resolution face-to-face?
"It should be said:
'It might be. In what way?
Here, monks, monks dispute:"

Whether it be "Dhamma" or "non-Dhamma," "Vinaya" or "non-Vinaya," "spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata" or "not spoken and not uttered by the Tathāgata," "practiced by the Tathāgata" or "not practiced by the Tathāgata," "prescribed by the Tathāgata" or "not prescribed by the Tathāgata," or "an offense" or "no offense."
"Whether it be a light offense or a heavy offense, an offense with remainder or an offense without remainder,
a grave offense or a non-grave offense—
if those monks are able to settle that legal issue, this, monks, is called a settled legal issue."
By what means is it settled?
By resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*).
And what is there in that resolution face-to-face?
Presence before the Saṅgha, presence before the Dhamma, presence before the Vinaya, and presence before the individuals.
And what therein is presence before the Saṅgha?
As many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forth; and those present do not protest.
This is, in that case, the presence of the Saṅgha.
And what, in that case, is the presence of the Dhamma and the presence of the Vinaya?
It is by whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, and by whatever teaching of the Teacher that particular legal issue is settled.
This is the presence of the Dhamma and the presence of the Vinaya therein.
And what is the presence of the persons therein?
He who disputes and he with whom he disputes—both adversaries being present face to face.
This is the presence of the person in that case.
Monks, if a legal issue that has been thus settled is reopened by the one who initiated it, there is an offense of expiation for the reopening;
if the giver of consent reviles it, there is an offense of expiation for the reviling.
If those monks, bhikkhus, are not able to settle that legal issue in that residence, they should go to whatever residence where there are many monks.
If those monks, while going to that residence, are able to settle that legal issue along the way, this, bhikkhus, is called a settled legal issue. By what has it been settled? By the path.
By means of resolution face-to-face.
And what, in this context, is resolution face-to-face?
It is presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individuals concerned.
And what therein is "presence before the Saṅgha"?
As many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the formal act have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forward;
and those present do not protest—this is "presence before the Saṅgha" therein.
And what therein is presence of the Dhamma and presence of the Vinaya?
That Dhamma, that Vinaya, and that teaching of the Teacher by which that legal issue is settled—
this is therein presence of the Dhamma and presence of the Vinaya.
And what therein is face-to-face with persons?
Both he who disputes and he with whom he disputes—the adversaries to the matter—are present together;
this is what is meant by "face-to-face with persons" in that context.
If, monks, a legal issue that has been thus settled is reopened by the one who initiated it, there is an offense of expiation for reopening it;
if the one who gave consent reviles it, there is an offense of expiation for reviling it.
And if, monks, those monks, while coming to that residence, are unable to settle that legal issue on the way—

But if, monks, the resident monks are junior and the visiting monks are senior, those resident monks, monks, should say this to the visiting monks:”
“In that case, venerable friends, please stay right here for a moment while we deliberate.
But if, monks, while the resident monks are deliberating, it occurs to them:
“We are not able to settle this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction,” then that legal issue must not be accepted by the resident monks.
But if, monks, while the resident monks are deliberating, it occurs to them:
“We are able to settle this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya,
and the Teacher’s instruction,” then those resident monks, monks, should address the visiting monks as follows:
“Venerable sirs, if you will report this legal issue to us exactly as it arose and exactly as it occurred,
and if we settle this legal issue according to the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction,
then it will be properly settled.”
"In this way we shall accept this legal issue.
If you, venerable sirs, do not report this legal issue to us exactly as it arose and exactly as it occurred,
then we shall resolve this legal issue according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction."
‘It will not be easily settled; we shall not accept this legal issue.
It is in this way, monks, that resident monks should thoroughly take charge before accepting that legal issue.
Those visiting monks, monks, should address the resident monks as follows:
‘We shall report this legal issue to the venerable ones exactly as it arose and exactly as it occurred.

If the venerable ones are able to settle this legal issue by means of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction—either within such a time or within such a period—it will be properly settled;
in this way we shall hand over this legal issue to the venerable ones.’

Venerable sirs, if you are not able to settle this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction— either within this much time or within that much time— it will not be properly settled; therefore,
we shall not hand over this legal issue to you.
‘We ourselves shall be the masters of this legal issue.
Having thus properly taken charge of it, monks, incoming monks should hand over that legal issue to the resident monks.
If those monks, monks, are able to settle that legal issue, this, monks, is called a settled legal issue.
By what is it settled?
By resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*).
And what is there in that resolution face-to-face?
Presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individuals...
[as before] ...If, monks, a legal issue that has been settled in this way is reopened by the one who initiated it, there is an offense of expiation for the one who reopens it;
if the one who gave consent reviles it, there is an offense of expiation for the one who reviles it.
9.2. Settlement by a Committee:

"Monks, if, while those monks are deciding that legal issue, endless discussions arise and the meaning of even a single statement is not understood, I allow you, monks, to settle such a legal issue by means of a committee."
To settle [a dispute] by means of a committee.
A bhikkhu endowed with ten qualities should be appointed to a committee:

he is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
He is learned, a retainer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning,
good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the entirely complete and pure holy life—
such teachings as these he has heard much of, remembered, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated by view.
Furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have been well-learned by him in detail, well-analyzed, well-mastered, and well-determined, both as to the rules and their detailed exposition;
he is firm and unshakable in the Vinaya;
and he is capable of comforting, persuading, convincing, inspiring, and gladdening both those who side with the truth and those who oppose it.
He is skilled in the arising and the settling of legal issues;
he knows the legal issue;
he knows the origin of the legal issue.
He knows the cessation of legal issues;
he knows the practice leading to the cessation of legal issues.
Monks, I allow you to appoint a monk endowed with these ten factors as a member of a formal committee.
And furthermore, monks, he should be appointed in this way:
first, a monk should be requested; having been requested, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me."
While this legal issue of ours is being decided, endless debates arise and the meaning of no single statement is understood.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha appoint the monk named so-and-so and the monk named so-and-so as a panel of judges to settle this legal issue.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
While this legal issue of ours is being decided, endless discussions arise and the meaning of what has been said by any single person is not understood.
The Saṅgha appoints the bhikkhus named so-and-so and named so-and-so as a committee to settle this legal issue."
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so and the monk named so-and-so as a panel for the settlement of this legal issue, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Saṅgha has appointed the monk named so-and-so and the monk named so-and-so as a panel for the settlement of this legal issue.
‘The Saṅgha consents; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
If, monks, those monks are able to settle that legal issue through a committee, this is called, monks, a settled legal issue.
By what means has it been settled?
By means of resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*).
And what, in this context, is resolution face-to-face?
It is presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the persons concerned … [and so forth] …
Monks, if a legal issue has been thus settled and a perpetrator reopens it, there is an offense of expiation for the one who reopens it.
Monks, while that legal issue is being decided by those monks, if there is a monk among them who is an expert in the Dhamma,
but neither the Sutta nor the Suttavibhaṅga has come to his mind, and he— failing to discern the meaning— relies on the shadow of the phrasing...
He obstructs the matter. A competent and capable monk should inform those monks:
"Venerable sirs, listen to me.
This monk named so-and-so is a preacher of the Dhamma."
Neither the Sutta nor the Suttavibhaṅga has come down for him.
Not discerning the meaning, he misinterprets the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing.
‘If it seems appropriate to the Venerable Ones, let us have the monk named so-and-so ordained and then settle this legal issue.’”
If, monks, those monks, having had that monk reinstated, are able to settle that legal issue, this is called, monks, a settled legal issue.
By what means was it settled?
By resolution in the presence of the parties (*sammukhāvinaya*).
And what, in this context, is face-to-face settlement?
It is presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the persons concerned...
[as before] ...If, monks, a legal issue thus settled is reopened by the one who initiated it, there is an offense of expiation for the one who reopens it.

If, monks, while that legal issue is being decided by those monks, there is a monk among them who is an expounder of the Dhamma, and although the Sutta has come down to him, the analysis of the Sutta (Suttavibhaṅga) has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [The formal motion follows: "Venerable sirs, let the Sangha listen to me. While this legal issue was being decided, a certain monk who is an expounder of the Dhamma—though the Sutta has come down to him, but not the Suttavibhaṅga—failing to discern the meaning, opposed the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing. "Venerable sirs, let the Sangha listen to me. While this legal issue was being decided, a certain monk who is an expounder of the Dhamma—though the Sutta has come down to him, but not the Suttavibhaṅga—failing to discern the meaning, opposed the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing. The Sangha authorizes the monk named so-and-so to recite the Suttavibhaṅga for the sake of settling this legal issue. If, while the Dhamma is being recited, there is another monk present who is an expounder of the Vinaya, and although the Dhamma has come down to him, the Vinaya has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [as above]. Then, monks, that monk who has been authorized by the Sangha should recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together for the sake of settling that legal issue. If, while the Dhamma and Vinaya are being recited together, there is another monk present who is an expounder of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and although the Dhamma and Vinaya have come down to him, the Aṭṭhakathā has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [as above]. Then, monks, that monk who has been authorized by the Sangha should recite the Aṭṭhakathā for the sake of settling that legal issue. If, while the Aṭṭhakathā is being recited, there is another monk present who is an expounder of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and although the Aṭṭhakathā has come down to him, the ancient tradition has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [as above]. If, while the lineage of teachers is being recited, there is another monk present who is an expounder of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and although the lineage of teachers has come down to him, the Dhamma has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [as above]. Then, monks, that monk who has been authorized by the Sangha should recite the Dhamma for the sake of settling that legal issue. If, while the Dhamma is being recited, there is another monk present who is an expounder of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and although the Dhamma has come down to him, the Vinaya has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [as above]. If, while the Vinaya is being recited, there is another monk present who is an expounder of the Dhamma and Vinaya, and although the Vinaya has come down to him, the Dhamma has not, and he, failing to discern the meaning, opposes the meaning based on the shadow of the phrasing, then a learned and competent monk should inform those monks: [as above]. Then, monks, that monk who has been authorized by the Sangha should recite the Dhamma and Vinaya together for the sake
‘Venerable sirs, listen to me.

9.3. The Majority Decision (Yebhuyyasikā) for Settling Disputes.
If those monks, bhikkhus, are unable to settle that legal issue by means of a committee, they should hand over that legal issue to the Saṅgha, saying:
"Venerable sirs, we are not able to settle this legal issue by means of a committee; let the Saṅgha itself settle this legal issue.
I allow you, bhikkhus, to settle such a legal issue by means of a majority decision (yebhuyyasikā).
A monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the distributor of voting sticks (*salākaggāhāpaka*):

one who would not follow a wrong course out of favoritism, nor follow a wrong course out of ill will, nor follow a wrong course out of delusion, nor follow a wrong course out of fear, and who would know what has been taken and what has not been taken...
And thus, monks, he should be appointed.
First, a monk should be requested; having been requested, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha should appoint monk so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks."
This is the motion.
Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs:
the Sangha appoints the bhikkhu named so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks.
Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of voting sticks, let him be silent;
whichever does not approve, let him speak.
The monk named so-and-so has been appointed by the Saṅgha as the distributor of voting sticks.
‘The Saṅgha consents; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Then that monk who distributes the voting sticks should distribute the sticks.
The legal issue should be settled according as the majority of monks speak in accordance with the Dhamma.”
This, monks, is called a legal issue that has been settled.
By what means was it settled?
By the presence of the accused and by a majority decision.
And what, in this context, is face-to-face resolution (*sammukhāvinaya*)?
It is: presence of the Sangha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individuals.
And therein, what is the presence of the Sangha?

When as many monks as are entitled to perform the legal act have arrived, when the consent of those who are entitled to give their consent has been brought forward, and when those present do not raise an objection—
this is the "presence of the Saṅgha" in that case.
And what therein is the "presence of the Dhamma" and the "presence of the Vinaya"?
By whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, and by whatever Teacher’s instruction that legal issue is settled—
that is the presence of the Dhamma and the presence of the Vinaya there.
And what is the presence of persons there?
Whoever disputes and that by which one disputes—both these adversaries who have come face to face are present here;
this is what is meant here by "presence of persons.
And what, in this case, is the majority decision?
Whatever constitutes the performance, the doing, the acceptance, the admission, the endurance, and the non-opposition of a *yebhuyyasika* (majority) legal act—
this is what constitutes *yebhuyyasika* in that regard. Monks,
if a legal issue settled in this way is reopened by the one who committed it, there is an offense of expiation for the one who reopens it.
"One who gives his consent is censured; for one who censures, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Now at that time, there was a legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that had arisen and come to pass in Sāvatthī in this way.
Then those bhikkhus,
being dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal case for the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī, heard:

"It is said that in such-and-such a residence there dwell many elder bhikkhus who are learned, of inherited knowledge, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, bearers of the Mātikā, wise, experienced, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training."
“If those elders were to settle this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, then this legal issue would be properly settled.
Then those monks went to that monastery and said to those elders:
“Venerable sirs, this legal issue has arisen in this way; it has come about in this way.”

"It would be well, venerable sirs, if the elders were to settle this legal dispute according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction, so that this legal dispute may be properly settled.
Then those elders,
[perceiving] that the legal dispute had been properly settled just as it was settled by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī—
In that way, they settled that legal issue.
Then those monks were dissatisfied with the settlement of the Sangha’s legal issue at Sāvatthī, and they were dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal issue by the many elders.
They heard: "It seems that in such-and-such a residence three elders are dwelling...
[or] two elders are dwelling...

[or] one elder is dwelling—one who is learned, of inherited tradition, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, a bearer of the Mātikā, wise, competent, intelligent, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training."
“If that elder were to settle this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, then this legal issue would be well-settled.
Then those monks went to that residence and said this to the elder:
“Venerable sir, this legal issue has arisen in such a way; it has come about in such a way.”

“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Elder would settle this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction, so that this legal issue may be properly settled. Then that Elder—
just as the Sangha at Sāvatthī had settled the legal issue, and just as many Elders had settled the legal issue—
"It was settled; it was well settled, just as a legal issue was settled by three elders and just as a legal issue was settled by two elders"—
in this way he settled that legal issue.
Then those bhikkhus were dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal dispute by the Saṅgha at Sāvatthī;
they were dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal dispute by a number of elders; they were dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal dispute by three elders;
they were dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal dispute by two elders; they were dissatisfied with the settlement of the legal dispute by a single elder.
They approached the Blessed One, and having approached, they reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
"Monks, this legal issue has been settled; it is stilled, calmed, and thoroughly pacified.
Monks, for the sake of reconciling those monks, I authorize three ways of taking voting sticks."
The secret ballot, the whispering in the ear, and the open ballot.
And how, monks, is there a secret ballot?
That monk who is distributing the ballots, having made the ballots of various colors, should approach each monk one by one and speak to him thus:
‘This is the voting ticket for one who speaks thus; this is the voting ticket for one who speaks thus.
Take whichever you wish. Once it has been taken, he should be told:
‘And do not show it to anyone.
If he knows:
‘Those who speak contrary to the Dhamma are in the majority; this is a wrong grasp,’ it should be withdrawn.
If he knows:
"Those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority," it is well-grasped;
the announcement should be made. This, monks, is how the secret ballot is conducted.
And how, monks, is there a voting by means of whispering into the ear?
That monk who is conducting the vote must whisper into the ear of each individual monk:
"This is the voting stick for one who speaks thus; this is the voting stick for one who speaks thus."
"Take whatever you wish. Once it has been taken, he should be told:
"Do not tell anyone."
If he knows:
"Those who speak contrary to the Dhamma are in the majority; this is a misapprehension," it should be withdrawn.
If he knows: ...
"If those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority," it is well-grasped; [the decision] should be announced.
This, monks, is how the voting by whispering into the ear is conducted.
And how, monks, is the voting by open ballot conducted?
If he knows:
"Those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority," he should have the ballots distributed openly and with full disclosure.
In this way, monks, the ballot distribution is conducted openly.
“Monks, these are the three ways of taking voting tickets. 9.5.
Resolution through Mindfulness:

A legal issue arising from an accusation is settled by four means of settlement:
by presence, by mindfulness, by restoration from insanity, and by a verdict of having committed a further offense.
It may be that a legal issue arising from an accusation is settled without resorting to two of these means of settlement.
The resolution for one who is no longer deluded and the further penalty for a grave offense—
would these two be settled by two methods of settlement:
namely, by resolution face-to-face and by resolution through mindfulness?
"It should be said:
'It might be. In what way?
Here, monks, monks groundlessly charge a monk with a failure in virtue."
Monks, when that monk has attained fullness of mindfulness, a verdict of mindfulness should be granted to him.

That monk, monks, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder... [and so on].
He should be addressed thus:
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhus are charging me with an unfounded failure in moral discipline.
Venerable sir, having attained fullness of mindfulness, I request the Saṅgha for a verdict of mindfulness.”
A second time he should be asked;
a third time he should be asked.

‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
The monks are accusing the monk so-and-so of a failure in virtue on groundless charges.

This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
The monks are accusing the monk so-and-so of a failure in virtue on groundless charges.
He, having attained fullness of mindfulness, requests the Saṅgha for a verdict of mindfulness.
The Saṅgha grants a verdict of mindfulness to the monk so-and-so who has attained fullness of mindfulness.

whichever does not approve, let him speak.
For the second time, I speak this matter... [as before]...
For a third time I speak this matter...
[as before] ...The Saṅgha has granted a verdict of mindfulness to the monk named so-and-so, who has attained fullness of mindfulness.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold it thus.
This, monks, is called a legal issue that has been settled.
By what means was it settled?
By resolution in the presence of the accused and by resolution through recollection.
And what, in this context, is face-to-face settlement (*sammukhāvinaya*)? It is: presence of the Saṅgha, presence of the Dhamma, presence of the Vinaya, and presence of the individuals...
What, in this context, is the presence of the individuals?
Whoever reproves and that which is reproved—both being present there:
this is the presence of persons in that case.

Whatever constitutes the performance, the carrying out, the acceptance, the admission, the acquiescence, and the non-objection regarding a legal procedure of resolution through mindfulness—
this is what pertains here to resolution through mindfulness. Monks,
if a legal issue settled in this way is reopened by the one who initiated it, there is an offense of expiation for the one who reopens it.
If one who gives consent becomes dissatisfied, there is an offense of expiation for that dissatisfied person. 9.6.

would these be settled by two methods of settlement:
by verdict in the presence of and by verdict of past insanity?

"I do not remember that;
it was done by me while I was deluded.

he should speak thus:
